A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MM-Nav and provide readable text, equations, tables, and figures supporting comparison. All nine pages of v1 and 29 pages of v2 were inspected. V1 ends with references; v2 adds an appendix in Section 6.

before.justification: V1 reports original IsaacLab evaluations, expert-combination and training ablations, and real-world robot demonstrations (Tables I–II and Figures 1, 5–6).

after.justification: V2 retains original experiments and adds public-benchmark evaluations, quantitative real-world ablations, latent-representation analyses, and RL training curves in the appendix.

M1.justification: Both versions use the same depth-based PPO experts, SigLIP/Qwen2-7B student, multi-view tokenization, continuous velocity head, joint action/VQA loss, and capability-balanced iterative training. VQA co-training already exists in v1. The appendix supplies previously unspecified details rather than establishing a changed algorithm.

E1.justification: V2 adds evaluation on InternVLA-N1 System-1 using InternScenes Home and Commercial environments. Real-world coverage expands to pedestrian interactions and outdoor low-light navigation. The original IsaacLab capabilities and several indoor demonstrations remain, including material retained under revised scenario names.

E2.justification: The new public-benchmark comparison includes DD-PPO, LoGoPlanner, InternVLA-N1(S1), and SIDP alongside iPlanner, ViPlanner, NavDP, and Mixed-RL (v2 Table 1). These additions substantially broaden the reported comparisons. The original IsaacLab comparator set remains unchanged in Table 2.

E3.justification: V2 introduces a public-benchmark protocol with 40 scenes, the benchmark's 100 start–goal pairs, Dingo embodiment, and SR/SPL metrics. It also adds controlled camera-view and VQA variants, 20 real-world trials per model/scenario, and latent analysis using 1,500 samples per domain. The original IsaacLab evaluation settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds direct VQA-removal and single-view ablations, representation comparisons at 0%, 50%, and 100% VQA, and quantitative real-world transfer tests. It extends the training-iteration analysis to the Mixed scene and adds expert convergence curves and rollout examples in the appendix. These substantially expand investigation of the method's components and generalization.

E5.justification: Neither version reports training-seed replication, across-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. V2's trial and sample counts specify evaluation sizes; its latent-density plots analyze representation distributions rather than uncertainty in performance estimates.

E6.justification: V1 Tables I–II are numerically retained as v2 Tables 2–3. V2 adds substantial results, including multi-view SR of 86.3/89.9 on Home/Commercial and real-world SR with versus without VQA of 55/0, 80/25, 70/20, and 85/10 percent (Figure 5). However, its claimed VQA-related drop exceeding 20% in both benchmark splits is unsupported by Table 1.

T1.justification: Appendix Section 6.2 adds explicit mathematical definitions for success and near-goal indicators, motion regularizers, reward components, and termination (Equations 8–11). V1 provides only the grouped reward and verbal component descriptions. The principal equations remain unchanged, and no theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The central contributions—multi-view navigation, specialized RL teachers, capability balancing, and student–expert synergy—remain intact. V2 foregrounds VQA co-training in the abstract and introduction and adds the explicit claim of 88.1% public-benchmark SR, extending the stated empirical scope without redefining the main proposal.

C2.justification: V2 substantially develops the transfer explanation: VQA is interpreted as aligning simulated and real action-relevant representations through exposure to real-image statistics (Figure 6). It also attributes poor RL-expert transfer to domain gaps and interprets the new view ablation in terms of spatial awareness. These extend v1's broader explanations based on VLA generality and expert synergy.

D1.justification: The new appendix specifies terrain construction, obstacle counts and dynamics, reset ranges, success thresholds, simulation timing, and PPO hyperparameters, including rollout length, learning rate, clipping, and optimization epochs. These are substantial reproducibility disclosures, not demonstrated changes to the original settings. New aggregate data totals are not reconciled with the retained per-stage counts and four refinement iterations.

R1.justification: V2 substantially broadens cited coverage of passive-video navigation, contemporary VLA/RL systems, and public benchmarks, including LeLaN, CityWalker, OmniVLA, InternVLA-N1, LoGoPlanner, and SIDP. The introduction expands positioning against real-data collection constraints and rule-based synthetic-data generation while retaining the original distillation and continuous-control distinctions.

P1.justification: V2 revises the abstract and introduction, adds an explicit contributions list and acknowledgements, and polishes or condenses several results paragraphs. Author and affiliation text also changes. The main section sequence and most method exposition remain recognizable; much of the expansion consists of new scientific material rather than wholesale rewriting.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column layout. Figures 1–3 are substantially redesigned to show the existing VQA pathway; Figure 4 gains a WTT panel, and the former Figure 6 gains a Mixed-scene panel as Figure 7. V2 also adds the public-benchmark table, latent plots, expanded real-world displays, and appendix tables and figures.

improvement.justification: V1 relies mainly on custom simulation tests and qualitative real-world demonstrations, without directly testing VQA's contribution. V2 adds public-benchmark validation, controlled VQA/view ablations, quantitative real-world trials, and substantial RL reproducibility details, strengthening central generalization claims. Percentage overstatements and unreconciled training-data totals reduce reporting precision, but do not outweigh these substantive gains.
